text.t: ATP, adenosine triphosphate, is the cell's energy-supplying molecule.
It is built from three parts: adenine, the sugar ribose, and a tail of three phosphate groups.
This flat double ring of carbon and nitrogen is adenine, the same base that spells the letter A in DNA.
The five-sided ring is the sugar ribose; adenine plus ribose together make adenosine.
The three phosphate groups are named alpha, beta and gamma, counting outward from the sugar.
Splitting off the gamma phosphate leaves ADP and a free phosphate, and releases energy the cell can use.
The bonds linking the phosphates are called high-energy bonds.

does.t: ATP supplies the energy for many reactions and processes inside cells.
Myosin uses ATP to power muscle movement, and actin uses it to build its filaments.

shape.t: Its formula is C10H16N5O13P3, and the three phosphorus atoms all sit in the phosphate tail.
Breaking ATP into ADP and phosphate releases energy because the products hold much less free energy than ATP and water.
The reaction can run the other way too: cells rebuild ATP by adding a phosphate back to ADP.

text.t: Most ATP is made in mitochondria by ATP synthase, using energy released from food.
The energy in glucose is used during cellular respiration to make ATP.

compare.t: From its farthest atom to its farthest atom, ATP measures about 1.7 nm.
ATP synthase, the machine that makes it, measures about 13.6 nm in this gallery, and that is only its head.

text.t: The outermost phosphate, the one removed to make ADP.
This oxygen links the beta and gamma phosphates.
